content: MT-ATP8, also known as ATP8, is a mitochondrial gene formally named mitochondrially encoded ATP synthase membrane subunit 8. This gene encodes a protein subunit of mitochondrial ATP synthase, specifically the ATP synthase Fo subunit 8, also referred to as subunit A6L. This subunit is part of the Fo complex within the larger F-type ATP synthase enzyme, which is also known as Complex V. Complex V is responsible for the final step of oxidative phosphorylation in the electron transport chain. One part of ATP synthase facilitates the movement of positively charged ions, or protons, across the inner mitochondrial membrane. Another part of the enzyme uses the energy generated by this proton flow to convert adenosine diphosphate (ADP) into adenosine triphosphate (ATP), the primary energy currency of the cell. The sequence of subunit 8 varies significantly between Metazoa, plants, and fungi. The MT-ATP8 gene is located in the mitochondrial genome and encodes the ATP synthase protein 8 in humans and other mammals. When the human mitochondrial genome was first sequenced, MT-ATP8 was initially identified as an unidentified reading frame (URF A6L). A unique feature of this gene is its 46-nucleotide overlap with the MT-ATP6 gene. The MT-ATP6 gene begins in a different reading frame (+3) relative to the MT-ATP8 reading frame (+1). The MT-ATP8 protein has a molecular weight of 8 kDa and consists of 68 amino acids. It is a subunit of the F1Fo ATPase, also known as Complex V, which is composed of 14 nuclear-encoded subunits and 2 mitochondrial-encoded subunits. F-type ATPases are divided into two structural domains: the F1 domain, which contains the extramembranous catalytic core, and the Fo domain, which contains the membrane-embedded proton channel. These domains are connected by a central stalk and a peripheral stalk. MT-ATP8 is part of the non-catalytic, transmembrane Fo portion of the complex, which forms the proton channel. The catalytic portion of mitochondrial ATP synthase is composed of five subunits (alpha, beta, gamma, delta, and epsilon) in a stoichiometric arrangement of three alpha, three beta, and one of each of the other subunits. The proton channel is made up of three main subunits (a, b, and c). The MT-ATP8 gene encodes the delta subunit of the catalytic core. Alternative splicing of this gene has been observed, but all variants encode the same protein isoform. The MT-ATP8 gene plays a critical role in mitochondrial ATP synthase, which is located in the inner mitochondrial membrane and the thylakoid membrane. This enzyme catalyzes the synthesis of ATP by utilizing the electrochemical gradient of protons across the inner mitochondrial membrane during oxidative phosphorylation. The Fo region of the enzyme drives the rotation of the F1 domain, which contains a water-soluble catalytic component that hydrolyzes ATP. Together, the F1Fo complex creates a pathway for proton movement across the membrane. In yeast mitochondrial F-ATPases, the MT-ATP8 protein is an integral component of the stator stalk, which is anchored in the membrane and prevents unnecessary rotation of the ATPase subunits relative to the rotor during ATP synthesis or hydrolysis. It is believed that MT-ATP8 serves a similar function in Metazoa. The nomenclature of ATP synthase has a historical basis. The F1 fraction is named Fraction 1, while the Fo fraction (written as a subscript o, not the numeral zero) is named for its ability to bind oligomycin, a naturally occurring antibiotic that inhibits the Fo unit of ATP synthase. The Fo region of ATP synthase is a proton pore embedded in the mitochondrial membrane. In humans, it consists of three main subunits (A, B, and C) and six additional subunits (d, e, f, g, MT-ATP6, and MT-ATP8). The three-dimensional structure of the E. coli homolog of this subunit has been modeled using electron microscopy data, forming a transmembrane four-α-helix bundle. Mutations in the MT-ATP8 gene, as well as other genes involved in oxidative phosphorylation, have been linked to various neurodegenerative and cardiovascular disorders. These include mitochondrial complex V deficiency, Leber's hereditary optic neuropathy (LHON), mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with stroke-like episodes (MELAS), Leigh syndrome, and neuropathy, ataxia, and retinitis pigmentosa (NARP) syndrome. Mitochondrial disorders often vary in severity depending on the proportion of mitochondria in each cell that carry the genetic mutation. For example, individuals with Leigh syndrome due to MT-ATP6 mutations typically have a very high percentage of mutated mitochondria (90–95%), while those with NARP syndrome have a lower percentage (70–90%). These two conditions are thought to represent a spectrum of overlapping features rather than distinct syndromes. Mitochondrial complex V deficiency is characterized by a loss of function in Complex V of the electron transport chain, leading to a wide range of symptoms that primarily affect the nervous system and the heart. This condition can be life-threatening in infancy or early childhood. Affected individuals may experience feeding difficulties, poor growth, low muscle tone (hypotonia), extreme fatigue (lethargy), and developmental delays. Elevated levels of lactic acid in the blood (lactic acidosis) are common and can cause nausea, vomiting, weakness, and rapid breathing. Hyperammonemia, or high levels of ammonia in the blood, may also occur, potentially leading to encephalopathy and damage to other organs. Additional symptoms include ataxia, microcephaly, developmental delays, and intellectual disability. A frameshift mutation in MT-ATP6, caused by a cytosine insertion at position 8612, results in a truncated protein of only 36 amino acids. Two single-nucleotide polymorphisms (T > C) at positions 8610 and 8614 create a homopolymeric cytosine stretch. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a common feature of mitochondrial complex V deficiency, is characterized by thickening of the cardiac muscle, which can lead to heart failure. This condition can range from mild to severe and may involve extensive fibrosis, myocyte disarray, and left ventricular outflow tract obstruction. The m.8528T>C mutation, located in the overlapping region of the MT-ATP6 and MT-ATP8 genes, has been identified in multiple cases of infantile cardiomyopathy. This mutation alters the initiation codon of MT-ATP6 to threonine and changes tryptophan to arginine at position 55 of MT-ATP8. Infantile hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (CMHI) is another condition associated with mutations in MT-ATP6 and MT-ATP8. This disorder is characterized by asymmetric thickening of the ventricular walls, often involving the interventricular septum. Symptoms include shortness of breath (dyspnea), fainting (syncope), collapse, palpitations, and chest pain, which are often triggered by physical activity. The clinical presentation of this condition varies widely, ranging from benign to severe forms with a high risk of heart failure and sudden cardiac death.
